title: The month of Magh
hookLine: in Magh, bathe in the dust of the holy (Barah Maha, ang 135)

lines: A BATH, BUT NOT IN A RIVER.
cards: Cold water at dawn, in the middle of winter. In north India, Magh, roughly mid-January to mid-February, is a month of bathing: Hindu tradition prizes a dawn dip in a river in Magh as an act of devotion.

Sikhs mark the month's first day with Maghi, and at Muktsar in Punjab people bathe in the sacred pool to remember the Forty Liberated, the Sikhs tradition says fell there in battle beside Guru Gobind Singh.
So when Guru Arjan reached Magh, his listeners already had water on their minds. And the bath he describes isn't in a river at all.

teach.b: The stanza opens maagh majan sang saadhoo-aa, dhoorree kar isnaan. In paraphrase: in Magh, let your bathing be in the company of the holy; make their dust your bath. Majan is bathing.

teach.h: DHOORREE: THE DUST OF THEIR FEET.
teach.b: Dhoorree is dust, the dust from the feet of the holy. It's a startling image, since dust is usually what a bath removes. But in Punjabi devotion, the dust of the feet is the sign of the lowest place.

To touch it is to make yourself small: I'll sit below you, I'll learn from you. So the bath that makes you clean, in this stanza, is humility. Then: meditate on the Lord's Name, listen to it, and give it to everyone.
The filth of past deeds washes off, and pride leaves the mind.
And the merit of all sixty-eight pilgrimage places, it says, is found in compassion for living beings. That's the turn. The stanza doesn't mock the river, or the people standing in it at dawn.
It moves the bath. Wherever you are, you can bathe this way: sitting low among good people, hearing the Name, being kind to anything alive. A Sikh habit catches this.
In the gurdwara, people sit on the floor, often near the door where shoes are left, and volunteers clean those shoes for strangers as seva. It's the dust of the feet, made practical.
Magh's bath ends where all baths end: you come out lighter. The stanza says it's pride you've washed off.

how: Sikhs mark the first of Magh as Maghi, and many bathe in the sarovar at Muktsar to remember the Forty Liberated; gurdwaras read Guru Arjan's Magh stanza, and serving the sangat, even cleaning shoes, is a common act of humility.

o: the first day of the month, kept at Muktsar
a winter month whose true bath is humility
the dust a dawn bath is meant to wash off

games.q: the month of Magh — tap the pairs.
p: the dust of the holy ones' feet
the first of Magh, remembered at Muktsar

s: the Magh stanza mocks people who bathe in rivers
it doesn't mock the river; it moves the bath into holy company and compassion.
in the stanza, the bath washes off pride
hearing the Name in holy company, it says, takes pride from the mind.
in Punjabi devotion, the dust of the feet is a sign of honor for others
to touch it is to take the lowest place and learn.

games.q: it's Magh, the month of bathing. where does Guru Arjan's stanza say to take your bath?
o: in the coldest river you can find, at dawn.
in the company of the holy, in the dust of their feet.
games.why: maagh majan sang saadhoo-aa, dhoorree kar isnaan: bathe in the company of the holy, with their dust. the stanza says this washes off pride.

practice: At a sink, or in your mind, feel the water's temperature on your hands, then bring it slowly to your face: the cool, the drip, the skin waking up.
As you dry your face, set down one small pride you've been carrying today, being right, being busy, being better at something. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Magh. In the Barah Maha, Magh's bath is taken in the company of the holy, in the dust of their feet, and it washes off pride.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dhoorr, dust. Gurbani often writes ਧੂੜੀ, dhoorree, the dust of the holy ones' feet.

carryVoice: Your line: magh: humble bath. Here, the cleanest bath is the lowest seat. That's five hundred seventy-six.
